title: The join key
goal: What `+` means, why one key can be both a word and an ending, and where it is used.

blocks.x: Every stroke after the first of a word carries the join key `+` (the left index finger's inner column: `T` and `G` on a keyboard). A stroke without it always starts a new word: boundaries are written, never inferred.
One key, a word and an ending
The right-hand `D` is both *do* and *-ed*. Only the join key decides which.

head: Strokes
Reads
rows: *end do* (without `+`, the same two keys are two words)

blocks.x: Without a join key the suffix takes the bare key (Plover's `-D` is always `{^ed}`), so *do* cannot have it. Here a word and an ending share the key, for many keys:
An ending can be one key, and the commonest words keep the cheapest keys.

items: A continuation stroke (a suffix struck on its own, or the consonants of a syllable that did not fit on the stroke before) is never a word, so it can be one key: [[+-G]] for *-ing*, [[+-D]] for *-ed*. It cannot collide with an unrelated one- or two-key word that has the same letters. See [the suffix table](#/ref/suffixes) and [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).
A suffix's own chord reads as its suffix after *any* stroke, dictionary entry or not. See [the solver](#/ref/fallback).
A stem's outline and a continuation stroke can share keys without clashing; only the join key tells them apart.
No vowel is dropped to mark a mid-word stroke, so *forget*/*forgot* pairs never collide over a boundary.

blocks.x: Keymux learns the join key from the steno layer's config: `extra_keys: ['+']` adds the key and `join_keys: ['+']` marks it as a join key (Keymux 1b9cf76 or later; the key's physical position goes in `layout_overrides`: `+` on the left index finger's inner column, the star on the right index only, and `overlay_overrides` draws `+` as its own column before the star; see below). A stroke with it down is only looked up glued onto the strokes before it. With no joined match (`TEST/+-D` does not exist), it falls back to its own entry; every suffix has one, defined as `{^text}`, so the ending still attaches to the previous word. See [the suffix table](#/ref/suffixes).
The physical layout, in the steno layer's config:

extra_keys: ['+'],
join_keys: ['+'],
layout_overrides: {
    "*": Key(KC_Y),        // star only on the right index
    "+": Key(KC_T),        // the join key on the left index (T) ...
    "+|G": Key(KC_G),      // ... and G
},
overlay_overrides: { "+": ColumnBefore("*") },

Strike `+` in every continuation stroke, or **hold it down** across them. Held, `+` stays in each stroke while the other keys come and go: each stroke is sent as its other keys come up, `+` included. `THAS`, then `+` held while striking `EUFG`, is `THAS/+EUFG`; a long word is struck syllable by syllable with `+` never released. Releasing `+` alone sends nothing. A word's first stroke is struck without `+`; only later strokes are joined.

`deploy` puts a small mod in the steno folder, the sticky-plus file (`06-lyk-sticky-plus.rs`). Each time a key comes up with others still down, the engine asks it whether to send the stroke now (its `send_early` hook); it says yes when `+` is the only key left. Needs a keymux with plugin `send_early` support; an older keymux does not load it, and `+` behaves as before (a stroke with `+` held goes when `+` comes up).
Lock (`+` alone) and the late star (`+*`)

**Lock: tap `+` on its own** inside a run and what the run types now is kept: the strokes after it only add to it, and the solver reads them as going on from it (`HRAOBG/+/+UP` is *look* kept, then *lookup*). Releasing a held `+` after its strokes is not a tap and locks nothing; tap it fresh. **`+*` puts the star on the stroke before**, struck late (`+-T` then `+*` is `+*T`). Both are the solver's: see [the solver](#/ref/fallback).

Wherever a page says a stroke "joins the one before it", "continues" or is a "continuation stroke", this key does it. Every way to build a word with it: [every way to join a word](#/ref/ways-to-join). Commands, punctuation and fingerspelling are pinned before any word gets an outline: see [reserved strokes](#/ref/reserved-strokes). [Lesson 10](#/lesson/10-endings) teaches endings by hand.
